title: Put a hand on your chest and say one kind sentence to yourself, the way you'd say it to a friend.
why: Self-kindness is linked to more resilience, not less drive.

title: Walk outside for 20 minutes, no headphones.
why: Walking in green places quiets the replaying thoughts.

title: Keep your phone in another room for the first 30 minutes after you wake up.
why: A slower start gives your attention back to you.

title: Write down three things that went well today, and why.
why: Noticing what went right, a few nights in a row, lifts mood for weeks.

title: Tidy one small corner: a drawer, a desk, a shelf. Stop at 15 minutes.
why: Small, finished tasks are an antidote to feeling stuck.

title: Block two hours with nothing productive in them. Protect them like a meeting.
why: Real rest is how you recover, not a reward for finishing.

title: Breathe slowly for 2 minutes: in for 4, out for 6.
why: Slow breathing with longer exhales helps your body shift into a calmer gear.

title: Drink a full glass of water, slowly, before your next coffee or scroll.
why: Even mild dehydration can drag on mood and energy.
evidence: Pross et al. 2014 (water intake and mood)

title: Walk up and down some stairs, or around the room, for 2 minutes.
why: A short burst of movement lifts energy more than a sugary snack.

title: Write down the worry that keeps looping, then one small thing you could do about it.
why: Putting a worry on paper turns a loop into something you can work with.

title: Notice one pleasant thing right now and stay with it 30 seconds longer than usual.
why: Savoring good moments makes them lift you more.

title: Set a wind-down alarm for 30 minutes before you want to be asleep tonight.
why: A cue to start winding down makes rest easier to protect.

title: Get 2 minutes of daylight: step outside or stand by a bright window.
why: Daylight helps set your body clock, which supports sleep and mood.
evidence: Blume et al. 2019 (light, sleep and mood)

title: Name what you're feeling in one or two words. That's the whole quest.
why: Putting a feeling into words can take a little of the sting out of it.

title: Write for 15 minutes about something that's been weighing on you. No one else has to read it.
why: Writing about hard things helps you make sense of them.

title: Move for 20 minutes in a way you actually enjoy: a dance video, a bike ride, a brisk walk.
why: Regular movement is one of the most reliable mood lifts there is.

title: Cook yourself a simple meal with a vegetable in it, and eat it without a screen.
why: Eating more fruit and veg is linked to better days, and cooking for yourself is care.
evidence: Conner et al. 2015 (fruit, vegetables and well-being)

title: Write a kind letter to yourself about something you've been hard on yourself for.
why: Self-kindness after a setback makes people more likely to try again.

title: Turn on do-not-disturb for 30 minutes and do something slow: read, stretch or just sit.
why: Real switching off is how energy comes back.

title: Spend 20 minutes in the nearest park or green space. Sit, stroll or just look at trees.
why: Time in green places adds up to better well-being.

title: Pack a picnic and a book and spend an afternoon outdoors somewhere green.
why: A long stretch in nature gets you most of a week's recommended dose in one go.

title: Plan a fully offline evening: phone off at 7, a good meal, a book or a bath, early to bed.
why: Detaching from screens and demands is how your mind recovers.

title: Take a two-hour walk somewhere green, no podcast, no destination.
why: Walks in nature quiet the thoughts that keep replaying.

title: Have a slow reset morning: sleep in, long breakfast, fresh sheets, no inbox until noon.
why: Choosing how you spend your time is a key part of recovery.

title: Try a beginner yoga, swim or dance class you've been curious about.
why: New movement brings a mood lift plus the fun of learning something.

title: Spend an afternoon making something with your hands just for you: bake, knit, build or paint.
why: Making things calms the body, whatever your skill level.

title: Spend an afternoon making your space feel good: open windows, fresh sheets, one cleared surface.
why: A home that feels restful is linked to lower day-to-day stress.
